title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The experiment used a shared‑initial generation: both conditions reused the same generated candidate and the guarded GVR pipeline could invoke at most one repair call per task. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call); execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d. Results: baseline 299/300 passes (0.9967), guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis (target effect 0.10, ≈80% power) was not supported: a ceiling baseline success rate and minimal repair engagement (repair invoked exactly once) made the preregistered detectable effect unattainable. We explain why the null result arises from these arithmetic and execution facts, explicitly identify where the single repair provider trace is archived for auditors, disclose which preregistered secondary estimands were not produced, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for stronger future confirmatory tests.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. Prior work shows LLMs can draft device configuration fragments yet still produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors; guarded pipelines that combine generation with deterministic verification and automated repair have been proposed to reduce operational misconfiguration risk. However, the community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that pair explicit intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration for confirmatory comparisons. To address this gap we preregistered and executed study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1: (1) a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) a snapshot deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) that enforces required sequence and workflow constraints, and (3) a paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass generator using a shared‑initial candidate design. Our final research question (preregistered) was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does GVR materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys document growing interest in LLMs for network management and emphasize core challenges—hallucination, prompt injection, and the need for verification—that bear on operational deployment [https://openalex.org/W4406137434, https://openalex.org/W4415071524, https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical work shows LLMs can synthesize router configurations but frequently need verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193, 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Tool‑assisted and generate–validate–repair (GVR) approaches can improve final correctness in focused prototypes [https://openalex.org/W4404652946], but these demonstrations are dataset‑specific and limited in scale. Security analyses of prompt injection and adversarial prompts further motivate guarded architectures and deterministic validators for operational NetOps workflows [https://openalex.org/W4405181600, https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. Our work contributes a sealed, archived proof‑of‑concept benchmark and a fully archived paired confirmatory run that ties a deterministic validator to an automated repair trigger under a tightly specified retry and budget policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary H1 asserted that the GVR pipeline would yield a higher per‑task validator pass rate than the frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration fixed task generation, validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, missingness treatment, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and an automated repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate). All design choices are archived.

Task bank generation. A deterministic generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, difficulty label, and a required_sequence that must appear in a valid candidate. Tasks span device counts 3–50 and use abstracted multi‑vendor models; no private data were used. The full task_manifest.jsonl is archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 062b80216e49a2919ebf8debd75cf02fffcfd752b5b253e5a11c0701ca853097).

Deterministic validator. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = v5.0) implements full_intent_constraint_validation as a stateless snapshot checker: it parses candidate commands to canonical field operations, enforces required_sequence and workflow_policies (ordering, mutual‑exclusion, group constraints), preserves unspecified state when requested, computes the implied final_state, and returns a binary pass/fail with diagnostic violation codes and a validator trace. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after traces, and validator.valid.

Shared‑initial paired design and repair budget. To isolate repair impact, each task produced a single shared initial candidate used as (a) the baseline single‑pass output and (b) the guarded pipeline's initial candidate. The guarded condition validated this candidate and, only on validator failure, could issue up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This shared‑initial + constrained‑repair policy was fixed in the preregistration and archived in execution/transformation_manifest.json.

Model configuration and determinism. The declared model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 produced deterministic provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Reproducing bit‑for‑bit hosted outputs therefore requires replaying that container or access to the identical provider model release and invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json.

Preregistered analysis. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The preregistered inferential test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness and sensitivity treatments (complete_pair_primary and failure_as_zero) were preregistered; the run completed with no missing or excluded pairs.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution manifest records: started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T12:41:43.384097+00:00, completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T13:07:38.995000+00:00, planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301, artifact_hash_count = 2108. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 301, stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}. These stage_counts document that the guarded repair stage executed exactly once across N=300 tasks.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. All analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Why the null arises (arithmetic ceiling). The exact McNemar test depends only on discordant pairs (n10, n01). Here n10 = 1 and n01 = 0 yield the reported two‑sided exact McNemar p = 1.0; this p‑value reflects the extremely small number of discordant pairs rather than evidence for equivalence in practical terms and is therefore uninformative in this ceiling setting. The paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (reported above) provides a more directly interpretable summary of practical uncertainty under the observed margins. Crucially, with baseline ≈0.9967 the pre‑specified target improvement of 0.10 is arithmetically impossible: the maximum achievable absolute paired gain given the observed baseline margin is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333, equal to the observed difference. Thus the preregistered target effect could not be realized under the sealed shared‑initial + single‑repair budget design.

Location of the single repair trace and discordant pair. The single repair provider invocation and its archived provider trace are contained in the authoritative execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json cross‑reference staged provider calls; auditors can deterministically locate the single repair record by filtering execution/raw_results.jsonl for the entry with stage == "repair" (there is exactly one such entry in the archived container). That repair record includes the pair_id field and the per‑call provider trace needed to verify the repair invocation. The execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) provides timestamps and stage indices that deterministically identify that single repair entry within execution/raw_results.jsonl. (We do not reproduce the raw provider trace inline in the paper; the archived raw_results.jsonl is the authoritative artifact.)

Representative diagnostic examples. Representative per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json) illustrate validator traces, normalized configurations, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, difficulty labels and validator.valid flags; they appear in the archival bundle and exemplify the required_sequence patterns used by the validator. The full raw_results.jsonl contains the single repair trace and the discordant pair index for auditors to inspect.
sections.discussion:
Interpretive scope of the null. The confirmatory null applies strictly to the sealed design (deterministic synthetic tasks; shared‑initial generation; snapshot deterministic validator; repair budget ≤1). Under these constraints the guarded GVR pipeline rarely differed from the baseline single‑pass candidate because the initial generator satisfied the validator for 299/300 tasks; hence the guarded pipeline could produce only negligible improvement. This outcome does not imply GVR architectures are generically unhelpful; rather, it quantifies that when generator quality is near ceiling and repair budgets are tightly constrained, localized repair yields minimal marginal benefit.

Practical recommendations grounded in archived artifacts. The execution artifacts support explicit, implementable modifications that make repair efficacy measurable in future confirmatory runs: (A) increase task difficulty or inject adversarial seeds to raise initial failure rates (the execution logs show 299/300 initial passes); (B) allow iterative repair budgets per failed candidate (stage_counts indicate repair=1 here, effectively inert); (C) permit multiple independent initial generations per task when evaluating selection/reranking strategies rather than repair efficacy; (D) adopt stateful/emulation validators that model ordered side effects and temporal constraints to expose runtime failure modes; (E) include explicit adversarial prompt/test cases to exercise prompt‑injection defenses. Each recommendation maps directly to observed execution facts and archived per‑task diagnostics.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variance but does not evaluate multi‑sample baselines or independent guarded sampling strategies; the repair stage executed only once, limiting internal contrasts. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 is a snapshot checker enforcing required_sequence and workflow_policies but does not model vendor CLI idiosyncrasies or asynchronous side effects; some real‑world failure modes could be missed. External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor) and only one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator version (v5.0) were evaluated; results do not generalize to production networks or other models without further experiments. Conclusion validity: the small number of discordant outcomes (n10=1) leaves subgroup and failure‑mode inference underpowered.

Preregistered secondary estimands and archived execution. The preregistration listed secondary estimands including per_task_failure_rate_guarded, per_task_failure_rate_baseline, and effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions. The archived analysis artifacts show secondary_results = [] (analysis/results.json and analysis/ directory), i.e., no separate preregistered secondary estimand outputs were produced by the registered executor beyond the primary confirmatory table and the bootstrap CI. This omission is an execution fact recorded in the archive (analysis/results.json) and is largely a consequence of the ceiling margins and absence of discordant variation; it reduces the set of confirmatory inferences that can be drawn from this run and is disclosed here to preserve transparency.

Operational implication. For practitioners: when generator quality is high and repair budgets are tightly limited, guarded repair mechanisms may offer little marginal benefit; in contrast, when generator reliability is lower, tasks are adversarial, or repair policies permit iteration/multiple alternatives, GVR pipelines are more likely to yield measurable operational gains. The public artifact bundle enables practitioners to instantiate these harder settings without rebuilding baseline infrastructure.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported; this outcome is explained by a ceiling baseline and minimal repair engagement (stage_counts show shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1). We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw provider traces (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...), per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable the community to extend the benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons that can demonstrate when GVR pipelines yield measurable operational value.

Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implementing scoring rule "full_intent_constraint_validation"; per‑task scorer outputs and validator traces are archived under execution/scoring/*.json. Preregistered analysis executor: paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar and paired bootstrap CI; bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}. The single repair provider trace and the corresponding discordant episode identifier are archived and indexed in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and in the execution manifest; auditors can extract the exact per‑item pair identifier and the standalone provider_call artifact by filtering the raw_results container for the entry with stage == "repair" and using the execution manifest cross‑references. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...).

Preregistered secondary estimands: several preregistered secondary estimands (for example, effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions and other secondary_results listed in the preregistration) produced no archived outputs in analysis/ (analysis/ secondary_results is empty); this absence is recorded in the analysis artifacts and reduces the set of confirmatory inferences derivable from this run.
